content.overview: Section 15 provides that “coercion” is the committing, or threatening to commit, any act forbidden by the Indian Penal Code (45 of 1860), or the unlawful detaining, or threatening to detain, any property, to the prejudice of any person whatever, with the intention of causing any person to enter into an agreement.
content.glance: Coercion = IPC-forbidden act or threat, or unlawful detention/threat to detain property, to prejudice of any person, intending to cause entry into an agreement.
content.study: Coercion is (1) committing or threatening to commit any act forbidden by the IPC, or (2) unlawful detaining or threatening to detain any property, to the prejudice of any person whatever, with the intention of causing any person to enter into an agreement. Consent caused by coercion is not free (s. 14) and the agreement is voidable (s. 19). Current-law framing: identify the act or threat; link to IPC or unlawful detention of property; prove intention to cause entry into the agreement; conclude on voidability.

sections.heading: IPC-forbidden act or threat
sections.body: Committing or threatening to commit any act forbidden by the Indian Penal Code.

sections.heading: Unlawful detention of property
sections.body: Unlawful detaining or threatening to detain any property.

sections.heading: Prejudice and intention
sections.body: To the prejudice of any person whatever, with the intention of causing any person to enter into an agreement.

examples.title: Threat of IPC offence
examples.body: A threatens B with an act forbidden by the IPC unless B signs an agreement. B’s consent is caused by coercion under s. 15.

hypotheticals.question: Must the threatened person be the one entering the agreement?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Coercion may be to the prejudice of any person whatever, with intention of causing any person to enter into an agreement.

misconceptions.trap: Only physical force against the contracting party counts as coercion.
misconceptions.correction: Section 15 covers IPC-forbidden acts/threats and unlawful detention of property, to the prejudice of any person, with the requisite intention.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should a Section 15 problem be analysed?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. Identify act/threat or detention. II. Link to IPC or unlawful property detention. III. Prove prejudice and intention to cause entry into agreement. IV. Conclude voidability under s. 19.

examTips: Quote the IPC limb and the property limb.
